units.translation: In the first passage the scholiast explains it as συγγενικάς [kindred], in the second as τὰς πρὸς εὐμένειαν Ἀγαμέμνονος [those for the goodwill of Agamemnon], in the third as τῆς ἐπὶ κηδεία τετμημένης [of the one honored at the funeral]. Since κῆδος [care, grief] means not only affinity but also mourning or grief, there is no doubt that Aeschylus called κηδείους χοάς [funeral libations] the libations to be offered to the dead, and κήδειον τρίχα [mourning lock] the hair to be placed on the tomb to signify grief, although κήδειος [connected by marriage, kindred] is also used for συγγενικός [kindred], on which see Thes. vol. 4 p. 1504.
pouring these funeral libations on the tomb
then she sends these funeral libations, hoping for a remedy that cuts away her woes
seeing this cutting of the mourning lock
those for the goodwill of Agamemnon
of the one honored at the funeral
if there is any guardian of these exiles
On this meaning see Thes. vol. 4 p. 1507.
to marry within one's own rank is by far the best
to care for, be concerned about
to care for, be concerned about
guard the city and care for it openly
faulty reading: for the meter requires an iambic dimeter, such as that which I have restored by uncertain conjecture: δύστανος ἁ κηδεμονία [wretched the guardianship].
grievous cares of the same name
and to Ilium a marriage connection with a true name was driven by the wrath that fulfills its purpose
nourishing the ever-new dye of much purple, worth its weight in silver
in the pitchy dye of flame
and the stain of blood in time is compounded
a lichen – will cast man-destroying stains upon the land

Aeschylus in Lycurgus (fr. 124) allegorically called the bonds κημούς [muzzles] in these words. On the κημῷ [muzzle] of horses see Xenoph. On Horsemanship 5, 3 with Schneider's note on 10, 5 and Jacobs p. 130-133. But Aeschylus seems to have spoken figuratively of a man whose mouth was shut.
allegorically called the bonds muzzles in these words

Κηναῖον [Cenaeum] is a promontory of Euboea, where there is a temple of Zeus Κηναίου [Cenaean], mentioned by Sophocles Tr. 993 (where Κηναία κρηπίς βωμῶν [Cenaean foundation of altars]) and Apollodorus 2, 7, 7.
around the Cenaean shore of Zeus
It is always taken in a bad sense.
of the Sphinx, the destruction of Thebes.
which are also called so by others: see Thes. vol. 4 p. 1521.
having taken away the man-seizing doom (Oedipus) from the land
O you boastful and death-bringing Fates, the Erinyes
heavy is the doom of not obeying
beasts and mortals harm her (i.e. the maidens)
where Meineke conjectured κηρόπακτος [wax-fastened] (Doric for κηρόπηκτος) in Leutsch's Philologus vol. 20 p. 52.
